knowledgePoints.name: Who runs it decides whether you loop
knowledgePoints.teach:
Server toolsClient tools
declared byyouyou
executed byAnthropic, server-sideyour code, where it runs
loop iterationnone — the result is in the same responserequired
examplesweb_search, code_execution, web_fetchmemory, bash

A server tool's result comes back in the same response. There is nothing for your loop to do.

What you look for in that response is a server_tool_use block and a matching tool-result block — bash_code_execution_tool_result, for instance — sitting alongside the text blocks.

Client tools are the ordinary case, even when the SDK ships the schema and a runner for them: shipping a schema is not the same as running the code.

questions.q: Why does a server tool need no loop iteration?
options: It is executed before the request is processed
Anthropic runs it server-side and returns the result in the same response
It returns no result, only a status
The SDK loops internally on your behalf
questions.explain: The round trip happens inside Anthropic's request handling. You get text and tool results together.

questions.q: Which is a client tool?
options: web_search
code_execution
bash
web_fetch
questions.explain: bash runs where your code runs. The other three are executed server-side.

reviewQuestions.q: Which block type signals a tool Anthropic ran for you?
options: tool_use
server_tool_use
tool_result
thinking
reviewQuestions.explain: server_tool_use, paired with a matching tool-result block in the same response.

reviewQuestions.q: The SDK ships a schema and a runner for a tool. Does that make it a server tool?
options: Yes — anything the SDK provides runs server-side
No — execution location is what defines the category, and it still runs where your code runs
Only if you do not override the schema
Only when used with the tool runner
reviewQuestions.explain: Convenience is not location. Memory and bash ship with schemas and are still client tools.

knowledgePoints.name: A tool with a budget and a boundary
knowledgePoints.teach:
The built-in web search tool is declared like any other, with a name, a type, and two controls worth knowing:

  • a max-uses limit, capping how many searches one request may run,
  • allowed domains, narrowing where it may look.

The response mixes several block types: server tool-use and tool-result blocks, text, and citation blocks.

Inspect the citations to tell a sourced claim from Claude's own synthesis.

That distinction is the point of the feature. A paragraph summarising four sources contains claims traceable to a document and claims that are the model's own connective tissue, and only the citations distinguish them. Use it for current facts, source discovery, and fact-checking — where the organisation has enabled the capability.

questions.q: How do you keep the web search tool inside a set of trusted sites?
options: Instruct it in the system prompt
Set allowed domains on the tool
Post-filter the citations and retry
Use web_fetch instead
questions.explain: The tool takes an allowed-domains constraint — configuration, not instruction.

questions.q: What lets you show users where an answer came from?
options: The server_tool_use block's input
Citation blocks in the response
The usage field
stop_reason
questions.explain: Citations point at the source behind a claim, which is also how you separate sourced claims from synthesis.

reviewQuestions.q: What is max-uses for on the web search tool?
options: Capping how many searches a single request may run
Limiting results per search
Capping monthly spend on the account
Restricting how many domains may be searched
reviewQuestions.explain: A per-request budget on searches — cost and latency control for an agent that could otherwise search indefinitely.

knowledgePoints.name: A sandbox with no network
knowledgePoints.teach:
Code execution is a server tool that runs Python in an isolated Docker sandbox with no network access. Claude can execute code multiple times in one conversation.

The no-network property is the design constraint everything else follows from. The sandbox cannot download your CSV, and it cannot upload its chart.

The Files API is how data gets in and out.

  1. Upload the file once via the Files API; you get a file id.
  2. Reference the id in a container_upload block — the sandbox now has it.
  3. Generated files come back as file ids inside code_execution_output blocks; download them by id.

The Files API earns its keep independently: upload once, reference by id forever, rather than re-encoding the same base64 payload into every message.

questions.q: The code execution sandbox has no network. How does a CSV get into it?
options: Base64 in the message, decoded by the generated code
Uploaded via the Files API, then referenced by file id in a container_upload block
Fetched by the sandbox from a URL you supply
Mounted from your server over the control channel
questions.explain: Files API in, file id referenced. Fetching from a URL is exactly what no network rules out.

questions.q: What does the Files API buy you outside the sandbox case?
options: Longer retention of conversation history
Upload once and reference by id, instead of re-encoding base64 into every message
Automatic chunking for RAG
Cheaper input tokens for images
questions.explain: One upload, an id you reuse — a straightforward saving on repeated payloads.

reviewQuestions.q: How do files generated inside the sandbox reach you?
options: They are streamed as base64 in the text block
As file ids in code_execution_output blocks, which you download
They are written to a bucket you configure
They cannot leave the sandbox
reviewQuestions.explain: Out by id, the same way they went in.

knowledgePoints.name: Built in means the schema, not the behaviour
knowledgePoints.teach:
The text editor tool gives Claude file and directory manipulation: view a file or directory, view line ranges, replace text, create files, insert at a line, undo edits.

The schema is built into Claude. You must write the implementation.

Claude knows how to ask for these operations — the vocabulary and argument shapes are trained in, and you enable them with a versioned stub such as text_editor_20250124 (the exact identifier varies by model). What no part of Anthropic's infrastructure does is touch your filesystem.

So it is a tool definition with the body missing, and the body is where the safety lives: your executor should constrain paths and operations. An agent asking to replace text in /etc/passwd is a request like any other until your code declines it.

questions.q: The text editor tool is 'built in'. What exactly is?
options: The schema and the implementation — you just enable it
The schema only; you write the code that performs the operations
The implementation only; you write the schema
Neither — the name refers to Claude Code's editor
questions.explain: Claude knows how to ask. Performing the operation is entirely yours.

questions.q: What safety obligation comes with implementing it?
options: Rate-limiting edits per conversation
Constraining which paths and operations are permitted
Encrypting file contents in transit
Logging every view operation
questions.explain: Path and operation constraints. The tool can request anything; only your executor decides what happens.

reviewQuestions.q: Why does the schema stub carry a date, like text_editor_20250124?
options: It expires and must be renewed
The stub is versioned and varies by model
It records when your implementation was registered
It sets the cache lifetime
reviewQuestions.explain: Versioned by model — the identifier you pass depends on which Claude you are calling.

knowledgePoints.name: Adaptive thinking, and where effort lives
knowledgePoints.teach:
Extended thinking lets Claude reason step by step before responding, producing visible reasoning tokens alongside the answer.

On Opus 4.7 thinking is adaptive: there is no token budget to set.

thinking = {"type": "adaptive"}

output_config = {"effort": "high"}   # ← effort lives HERE, not beside thinking

effort goes inside output_config. Its values are low, medium, high (default), xhigh, max.

That placement is a favourite exam detail, because the intuitive guess — putting effort next to the thinking block it obviously controls — is wrong.

questions.q: Where does the effort parameter go?
options: Inside the thinking block, alongside its type
Inside output_config
At the top level of the request, beside max_tokens
In the system prompt
questions.explain: output_config — not next to the thinking block, despite controlling how deeply it thinks.

questions.q: What is the default effort level?
options: low
medium
high
max
questions.explain: high is the default, with low and medium below it and xhigh and max above.

knowledgePoints.name: When thinking is just latency
knowledgePoints.teach:
Turn it on for: mathematics and multi-step logic, code debugging, regulatory and trade-off analysis. Tasks where the route to the answer is the hard part.

Skip it for simple classification, extraction, and boilerplate. There it adds latency and cost and buys nothing.

There is a second, quieter cost: thinking arrives as a new block type in content. Any code indexing content[0].text starts reading reasoning where it expects the answer — the classic symptom of enabling thinking on a mature integration.

questions.q: Name a task where enabling thinking makes the product worse.
options: Debugging a failing test
Classifying a support ticket into one of five categories
Analysing a regulatory trade-off
Working through a multi-step calculation
questions.explain: Simple classification gains nothing from reasoning tokens and pays for them in latency and cost.

questions.q: You enable thinking and your UI starts showing reasoning instead of the answer. Why?
options: Thinking replaces the text block
A thinking block now precedes the text block, and the code reads content[0]
The answer is returned in a separate field
max_tokens is consumed before the answer begins
questions.explain: A new block type appeared ahead of the text. Loop and dispatch on block.type instead of indexing.

reviewQuestions.q: What changed about thinking on Opus 4.7?
options: It became free
It became adaptive — no token budget to set, just type: adaptive
It moved from the API to the SDK
It became the default for all requests
reviewQuestions.explain: Adaptive: the budget parameter is gone, and depth is expressed through effort instead.

knowledgePoints.name: Order, labels, and resolution
knowledgePoints.teach:
Images are content blocks in the messages array — base64 data or a URL — and one message can carry several. Supported: JPEG, PNG, GIF, WebP.

Three practices, each fixing a specific failure:

PracticePrevents
Put the image block before the text describing itClaude reading a description before it has seen what is described
Give multiple images clear labels or captionsambiguity when you later say “the second image”
Downscale when full resolution buys nothingpaying for input tokens you did not need

Higher resolution costs more input tokens. Resolution is a budget decision, not a quality default.

Images stay in context across turns, so Claude can refer back to one from an earlier message — as long as that message is still in the array you are sending.

questions.q: You send three photos and ask about “the second one”. What should you have done?
options: Sent them in separate messages
Labelled the images, and put each image block before the text describing it
Used URLs rather than base64
Downscaled them to a uniform size
questions.explain: Labels remove the ambiguity, and image-before-text is the ordering convention.

questions.q: What is the cost consequence of image resolution?
options: None — images are billed per image
Larger and higher-resolution images consume more input tokens
Resolution affects output tokens only
Only formats other than JPEG are billed by size
questions.explain: Resolution is input tokens, so downscale when the detail is not doing any work.

reviewQuestions.q: Can Claude refer to an image from an earlier turn?
options: No — images are discarded after the response
Yes, as long as that message is still in the array you send
Only if it was uploaded via the Files API
Only within the same message
reviewQuestions.explain: Same rule as everything else in a stateless API: it is in context if you resent it.

knowledgePoints.name: Layout is information
knowledgePoints.teach:
A PDF goes in directly as a document content block — base64 or URL. What comes back is not an OCR dump:

Claude reads both the extracted text and the visual layout — tables, charts, embedded images.

That is the reason to prefer it over running your own text extractor. A pre-extracted string flattens a table into a run of numbers and loses which column they were in; the document block keeps the structure that made them meaningful.

Costs and limits: page-count and file-size caps apply, and each page bills roughly like an image (visual tokens) plus its extracted text tokens. So a long PDF is a substantial context expense — which is the pressure that leads to RAG.

questions.q: A contract's meaning is in its tables. Why not extract the text yourself and send the string?
options: Extraction libraries are slower than the API
A flat string loses the layout — which column a number was in — that the document block preserves
Extracted text cannot be cached
The API rejects plain text over a size limit
questions.explain: The document block reads layout as well as text. Flattening a table is exactly the information you would lose.

questions.q: How is a PDF page billed?
options: As text tokens only
Roughly as an image, plus its extracted text tokens
A flat rate per page
As output tokens, since it is processed after the prompt
questions.explain: Visual tokens plus text tokens — which is why long PDFs get expensive fast.

reviewQuestions.q: When is sending a PDF as a document block clearly the right call?
options: Whenever the file is a PDF
When its visual structure — tables, figures — carries meaning a text dump would lose
Only when it is under one page
Only when citations are enabled
reviewQuestions.explain: The value is layout. For a plain prose PDF the difference is much smaller.

knowledgePoints.name: Two location types
knowledgePoints.teach:
Opt in per document block:

{"type": "document", "source": {...}, "citations": {"enabled": true}}

The response then includes citation blocks pointing at the exact source location behind each claim. Which kind of location depends on the source format:

typesourcepoints at
citation_page_locationPDFspage start / end
citation_char_locationplain textcharacter start / end index

Paged source, page location. Unpaged source, character offsets.

What this enables in a product: a user clicks a sentence in the answer and lands on the passage that supports it. It also makes an answer auditable — a claim with no citation is a claim the model supplied itself.

questions.q: You enable citations on a PDF. Which location type comes back?
options: citation_char_location
citation_page_location
citation_block_index
Both, for every claim
questions.explain: PDFs are paged, so citations point at page start and end.

questions.q: How are citations turned on?
options: A top-level request parameter
Per document block, with citations: {enabled: true}
In the system prompt
They are always on for document blocks
questions.explain: Per block, opt-in — so you can cite one source and not another in the same request.

reviewQuestions.q: What does a claim without a citation tell you?
options: The citation failed to generate
It is the model's own synthesis rather than something traced to a source span
The source document was too short to cite
Citations were disabled for that turn
reviewQuestions.explain: Citations mark the sourced claims, so their absence marks the connective tissue the model supplied.

knowledgePoints.name: The loop, wearing a camera
knowledgePoints.teach:
Computer Use lets Claude operate a computer the way a person does — view the screen, move the mouse, click, type, scroll, run shell commands — rather than calling purpose-built APIs. It is for software with no API: legacy applications, consumer GUIs, UI-level testing.

The loop is the agent loop with one substitution:

  1. You send a screenshot of the current screen, plus the task.
  2. Claude requests a computer action — screenshot, left_click, type, key.
  3. Your code performs it against the environment.
  4. You take a new screenshot and send it back as the tool result.
  5. Repeat until Claude decides the task is done.

Instead of a JSON tool result, the result Claude reads is a fresh image of what changed on screen.

Step 4 is environment inspection with nowhere to hide: Claude has no other way to know whether the click landed.

questions.q: What do you send back after performing a Computer Use action?
options: A JSON status object describing the action
A new screenshot, as the tool result
The mouse coordinates that were used
Nothing — Claude continues from its own plan
questions.explain: A fresh image is the tool result. It is the only way Claude perceives whether anything changed.

questions.q: Where must Computer Use run?
options: On the user's own desktop, for realistic testing
In a sandboxed VM or container, never a production desktop
On Anthropic's infrastructure, as a server tool
In a browser tab with restricted permissions
questions.explain: Arbitrary UI actions demand a sandbox. This one is not negotiable.

options: Speeding up API calls by batching them through a UI
Driving software that has no API, and automating UI-level flows
Running code in a sandbox without network access
Editing files on your server
reviewQuestions.explain: Legacy apps and consumer GUIs — the cases where no programmatic interface exists to call.

reviewQuestions.q: How does the Computer Use loop relate to the ordinary agent loop?
options: It is a distinct protocol with its own endpoint
It is the same loop, with a screenshot in place of the JSON tool result
It runs server-side and needs no loop
It replaces stop_reason with a screen-state check
reviewQuestions.explain: Same five steps, visual environment. The specialisation is what the tool result carries.
